meaning: You did something, and as a result you found out a fact or got a certain outcome. Like “I tried ..., and it turned out ...”.
connection: Verb た-form + ところ、+ result (usually something that already happened)

senses.label: Did it and found out
senses.meaning: The first part is an action the speaker did on purpose. The second part is the result or fact learned afterwards, often something new or surprising. The second part is in the past tense.
senses.connection: Volitional verb た-form + ところ、…た (common: 「調べたところ」, 「聞いてみたところ」, 「問い合わせたところ」)
examples: I asked a station attendant, and apparently the train is running 30 minutes late.
I looked it up online and found that the shop had already closed down.
I had a doctor examine me, and was told it was just a cold.

senses.label: Expected or unexpected result
senses.meaning: The result can be what you hoped for, or the opposite of what you expected. For an unexpected result you often see 「〜たところ、意外にも」. In written style you also see 「〜たところが」.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + ところ、(意外にも / 思ったより) …た
examples: I consulted my teacher, and they gladly agreed to help.
I tried a new method, and it went better than I expected.

notes: The second part is a fact you only learned after doing the action, so it must be stated in the past tense. It can't be an intention, an order or a request: ✕「調べたところ、行きましょう」→ ○「調べたところ、もう閉店していた」.

Three similar-looking phrases mean completely different things: 「行ってみたところ、休みだった」 (I went and found it was closed); 「今行ったところだ」 (I've just been there); 「今から行ったところで、間に合わない」 (even if I go now, I won't make it).
The first part is usually something the speaker did on purpose to find out about a situation (「調べる」「聞く」「頼む」「試す」). A natural event can't be the first part: ✕「雨が降ったところ、道がぬれていた」→ ○「外に出てみたところ、道がぬれていた」.
When reporting findings to a boss or client, 「確認したところ、〜でした」 sounds appropriately professional. 「確認したら〜だった」 sounds casual and conversational, so avoid it in formal emails.

daily.title: Reporting what you found out
daily.description: Telling your family what you learned on the phone.
daily.example: I called the restaurant, and they were fully booked today.

daily.title: Trying something new
daily.description: Sharing your impression with a friend after trying a product.
daily.example: I tried this toner, and my skin got better.

daily.title: Reading a news report
daily.description: News often uses it to present the results of an investigation.
daily.example: When residents were asked, it turned out that many people feel anxious.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Politely reporting the result after checking something.
work.example: I checked with the client, and they said the delivery date is next Friday.

work.title: Writing a survey report
work.description: Explaining the results of an experiment or survey in a report or paper.
work.example: When a questionnaire was conducted, about 70% answered that they were satisfied.

etymology: 「ところ」 is written 「所」 and originally means “place”. It extended to mean “moment, stage”. 「〜たところ」 first meant “at the moment I had done ...”, and then “after doing ... (I found)”, introducing a result.

similar.title: 〜たら〜た・〜と〜た (discovery)
similar.explanation: Both can mean "I did ... and found that ...". 「〜たら」 is casual and conversational, and the second part can be something you just happened to come across (「窓を開けたら雪が降っていた」). 「〜たところ」 is a bit more formal and is mostly used for results obtained after a deliberate investigation or inquiry, which makes it good for reports.

similar.title: 〜結果
similar.explanation: Both introduce the result of doing something. 「〜た結果」 stresses a final conclusion reached after effort, discussion or a process, and is strongly written in tone (「話し合った結果、中止になった」); 「〜たところ」 just means "I did it and learned that ...", and the result isn't necessarily the fruit of any effort.

similar.title: 〜ところだ
similar.explanation: Same root: both are built on 「ところ」. 「〜たところだ」 ends the sentence with 「だ」 and means "have just done" (「今着いたところだ」); 「〜たところ、…」 is followed by 「、」 and a result clause, meaning "I did ... and found that ...".

similar.title: 〜たところで
similar.explanation: Same root, but pointing the opposite way: 「〜たところで」 means "even if ..., (it's no use)", and the second part is usually a negative assessment (「謝ったところで、許してもらえない」); 「〜たところ」 introduces the result you actually got.

formation: 「〜たところ」 = verb た-form (the action is complete) + 「ところ」 (originally "place", here a point in time or a scene). Together they mean "at the moment when ... was done". Add 「、」 and another sentence, and you're saying "at the moment I finished ..., I (saw / learned) ...". So the second part is naturally a fact you only learned after the action, and since it has already happened, it's in the past tense. Because it means "learning something in that scene", the first part is usually a deliberate action such as investigating or asking to find out about a situation. In written style, adding 「が」 with its contrastive flavor gives 「〜たところが」, which more readily introduces an unexpected result.

meaning: Something else happens just when you are at a certain moment or in a certain situation. Often someone arrives or a call comes in, interrupting or affecting what is going on.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ている-form / た-form + ところに・ところへ; い-adjective + ところに

senses.label: Just when ..., someone came
senses.meaning: The first part is the situation the speaker is in; the second part is something that suddenly happens at that moment. The second part usually has a verb of movement or appearance, such as 「来る」, 「現れる」 or 「電話がかかる」. 「ところへ」 stresses the sense of “arriving” a bit more than 「ところに」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form (about to) / ている-form (in the middle of) / た-form (just finished) + ところに・ところへ + 来る / かかってくる etc.
examples: Just as I was about to go out, a friend came to visit.
A phone call came while I was taking a bath.
Just as we finished talking, the department manager walked in.

senses.label: Perfect timing
senses.meaning: 「いいところに」 and 「ちょうどいいところへ」 mean someone came at just the right time. Very common in conversation. It can also show that a situation gets worse: 「困っているところに、さらに〜」.
senses.connection: いい / ちょうどいい + ところに・ところへ + 来た; verb ている-form + ところに + さらに…
examples: Oh, you came at just the right time. Give me a hand.
While I was lost and didn't know what to do, a kind person spoke to me.

notes: The second part is something from outside that you don't control (someone arrives, the phone rings, it starts raining). It can't be your own intentional action: ✕「出かけようとしているところに、私は傘を取りに戻った」→ ○「出かけようとしているところに、雨が降ってきた」.

It's most often confused with 「ところを」. Use 「に／へ」 when the second part is something that comes into the scene, and 「を」 when it is an action done to the scene. ○「寝ているところに友達が来た」／○「寝ているところを友達に見られた」, ✕「寝ているところに友達に見られた」.
「いいところに来た」 is casual speech for friends or people below you, with a tone of "you're just in time to help me". Don't say it to a boss or client; say 「ちょうどご相談したいと思っていたところでした」 instead.
After a noun or na-adjective (「静かなところに住みたい」), 「ところ」 usually means a literal "place"; that's not this grammar point.

daily.title: A friend shows up at the right time
daily.description: A friend appears just when you need help.
daily.example: You came at just the right time. Help me carry this box.

daily.title: Interrupted during a meal

daily.example: A sales call came in while I was eating.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: Novels often use it to bring a new character on stage.
daily.example: While the two were talking, a strange man appeared.

work.title: Someone enters a meeting
work.description: Describing to a colleague what happened at a meeting.
work.example: Just as we were about to start the meeting, the president arrived.

work.title: More work when you're busy
work.description: Complaining to a colleague about work piling up.
work.example: I'm busy with a deadline, and on top of that I was given a new task.

etymology: 「ところ」 originally means “place”, and was extended to a point in time, “moment, scene”. Adding 「に」 or 「へ」, which mark direction or destination, gives “(something) came to this moment”, that is, “just when ..., ... happened”.

similar.title: 〜ところを
similar.explanation: Same root, and the one it's most often compared with. 「〜ところに／へ」 is followed by something that arrives or happens (「友達が来た」「電話がかかってきた」); 「〜ところを」 is followed by an action done directly to that scene, often in the passive (「見られた」「助けられた」).

similar.title: 〜最中に
similar.explanation: Both can mean "right while ... (something else happened)". 「〜最中に」 stresses being interrupted at the very height of something, and usually follows 「ている」 or "noun + 「の」"; 「〜ところに」 can also attach to the "about to" or "just finished" stages, and the second part is usually something like "someone came".

similar.title: 〜ところだ
similar.explanation: Same root. 「〜ところだ」 only says which stage an action is at (about to / in the middle of / just finished); 「〜ところに／へ」 adds an event that bursts in at that stage.

formation: 「〜ところに／へ」 = verb (dictionary form / ている-form / た-form) + 「ところ」 (a point or scene in time) + 「に」 marking the destination, or 「へ」 marking direction. The verb form decides which point: the dictionary form is "about to", the ている-form is "in the middle of", and the た-form is "just finished". 「に／へ」 treats this scene as a destination, so the second part is someone or something "arriving" at it; that's why the second part is so often 「来る」「訪ねてくる」 or 「電話がかかってくる」. And because something from outside barges in, the sentence often carries a sense of "being interrupted" or "turning up at just that moment".

meaning: Says that while someone was in a certain scene or situation, something was done to them by another (being seen, disturbed, helped, etc.); also used in polite set phrases (“at a time when you are busy...”) and for the contrastive “where one should have..., but instead...”.
connection: Verb dictionary / ている / た form, い-adjective, noun + の + ところを; (本来なら) verb dictionary / た form or 〜べき + ところを

senses.label: Caught while ...
senses.meaning: The first part is the scene someone is in; the second part is what another person does to that scene. Common verbs are 「見る」, 「見つかる」, 「呼び止める」 and 「起こす」, often in the passive. Usually unwelcome for the person.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form / dictionary form + ところを + 見られる / 見つかる / 捕まる etc.
examples: My teacher saw me sleeping in class.
I was stopped by a reporter just as I was leaving home.
The thief was caught by the police as he was running out of the shop.

senses.label: Rescued from trouble
senses.meaning: The second part can also be something good, such as 「助ける」 or 「救う」: being helped in a difficult or dangerous situation. It often carries gratitude.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form + ところを + 助ける / 救う; 危ない + ところを
examples: While I was lost, a kind person helped me.
Thank you very much for saving me when I was in danger.

senses.label: Polite: when you are ...
senses.meaning: Phrases like 「お忙しいところを」 and 「お休みのところを」 are used to apologize or thank someone: “(sorry to bother you / thank you) when you are so busy / resting”. Common in business and formal settings. 「を」 is sometimes dropped.
senses.connection: お忙しい / お疲れの / お休みの / ご多忙の + ところ(を) + すみません / ありがとうございます
examples: Sorry to bother you when you're busy. Do you have a moment?
I'm very sorry to disturb you while you're resting.
Thank you very much for coming today despite the bad weather.

senses.label: Where one would normally..., instead
senses.meaning: Normally the first part would happen, but the actual result is different. Often paired with 「本来なら」 or 「普通なら」. Usually expresses relief or gratitude.
senses.connection: (本来なら／普通なら) verb dictionary form / た-form + ところを、〜 (also 「〜べきところを」)
examples: I should have been punished, but this time I was forgiven.
It normally takes an hour, but I got there in thirty minutes.
I should visit you in person, but please excuse me for writing by email instead.

notes: In the set phrase used as a courtesy, always use honorifics with a boss or client: 「お忙しいところ（を）すみません」「お休みのところ申し訳ありません」. ✕「忙しいところをすみません」 sounds blunt and rude. You also can't use it about yourself: ✕「私の忙しいところを来てくれた」.

Don't reverse the direction in passive sentences: the person seen is yourself, and the one who sees takes 「に」. ○「寝ているところを先生に見られた」 (my teacher saw me sleeping); ✕「先生が寝ているところを見られた」 (this becomes "the teacher was seen sleeping").
Distinguish it from 「ところに」: use 「を」 only when the second part is an action done to the scene. ✕「寝ているところに先生に見られた」→ ○「寝ているところを先生に見られた」.
「〜ところを見ると」 means "judging from ... (I guess)", not "being seen": 「笑っているところを見ると、合格したらしい」.
In business email, 「本来ならば直接お伺いすべきところを、メールにて失礼いたします」 is a common polite formula. Dropping the first half and writing just 「メールで失礼します」 looks discourteous to a client.

work.example: Thank you all very much for gathering here today despite your busy schedules.

etymology: 「ところ」 originally means “place” and extended to “scene, moment, situation”. With the particle 「を」, either the scene is treated as the object of the main action (what is seen, caught or helped is “that scene of doing...”), or 「を」 marks passing through, as in 「道を歩く」 and 「橋を渡る」, i.e. “getting past this situation”, which gives the contrastive “should have..., but...”.
formation: 「〜ところを」 = verb / adjective / noun + の + 「ところ」 (scene, moment, situation) + the particle 「を」. 「ところ」 packages the preceding content as a “situation”, and 「を」 then makes that situation either the target of the following action or a place passed through; these two directions produce the senses here. First: 「を」 makes the whole scene “while doing...” the object of the following verb — what is seen, caught or helped is “a person in that scene”, so the main verb is a transitive verb that acts directly on its object (見る・見つける・捕まえる・助ける), and when the speaker is the person involved it becomes the passive 「見られた」「助けられた」. The polite 「お忙しいところを（お邪魔して）すみません」 has the same structure: the object of the omitted verb 「邪魔する」 is “the time when you are busy”, carrying an apology for disturbing you at just that time. Second: this 「を」 is generally understood as marking a place passed through, like 「道を歩く」 or 「橋を渡る」, so 「AところをB」 means “getting past the situation A to do B”: A is the situation that ought to hold (one ought to be punished, ought to visit in person), the speaker goes past it and B occurs, giving the contrastive “should have A, but B”.

similar.title: 〜ところに・〜ところへ
similar.explanation: Same root, and the easiest to mix up. 「〜ところに／へ」 is followed by something that arrives or happens (「友達が来た」); 「〜ところを」 is followed by an action done directly to the scene (「見る」「捕まえる」「助ける」).

similar.title: 〜最中に
similar.explanation: Both can mean "while ... (was ...ed)". 「〜最中に」 only says "in the middle of", and the second part can be anything that happens (「会議の最中に停電した」); with 「〜ところを」, the second part must be an action done to that scene.

similar.title: 〜ところを見ると
similar.explanation: Same root. 「〜ところを見ると」 means "judging from ...", and the second part is the speaker's guess (「〜らしい／〜ようだ」); in this grammar point, 「見る」 means really seeing the scene.

similar.title: 〜にもかかわらず
similar.explanation: Similar meaning. 「にもかかわらず」 means "in spite of... still" and is more objective, its first part being an established fact. In 「ところを」 the first part is "the situation that should have been", stressing "it should have been so, but actually it's like this".

meaning: Something (usually bad) almost happened, but it actually didn't. Like “nearly ...” or “almost ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + ところだった (often with 「もう少しで」, 「危うく」 or 「〜なかったら」)

senses.label: Nearly ...
senses.meaning: Something was about to happen but was avoided in the end. Usually something unwanted, with a sense of relief: “that was close”. Often used with 「もう少しで」, 「危うく」 or 「あやうく」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ところだった / ところでした
examples: I almost missed the train.
I nearly got hit by a car.
I overslept and was nearly late for an important exam.

senses.label: If not for ..., would have ...
senses.meaning: Used with conditions like 「〜なかったら」 or 「〜なければ」: “if it hadn't been for ..., ... would have happened”. Used to thank someone or to feel relieved about something.
senses.connection: 〜なかったら / 〜なければ + verb dictionary form + ところだった
examples: If you hadn't told me, things would have gotten really bad.
Without a map, I would have gotten lost.

senses.label: Was just about to ...
senses.meaning: No “nearly” meaning here. It is simply the past of 「〜ところだ」 (about to): at a past moment you were just about to do something. Context tells the two apart.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ところだった (often with 「ちょうど」)
examples: I was just about to call you.

notes: The event didn't actually happen, so you can't replace this with the plain past: ✕「危うく事故を起こした」 (this means you really caused an accident) → ○「危うく事故を起こすところだった」.
It must follow the verb dictionary form. 「ているところだった」 and 「たところだった」 only mean "was in the middle of" and "had just done"; they don't mean "almost".
The same 「〜ところだった」 can also just mean "was about to": 「ちょうど電話するところだった」 means "I was just about to call", not "I almost called". It means "almost" only with words like 「もう少しで」「危うく」 or 「〜なかったら」.
Saying 「教えていただかなかったら、遅刻するところでした。助かりました」 to someone who helped you is a natural way to thank them. If someone warned you and you only say 「大丈夫でした」, you'll come across as ungrateful.

daily.title: Telling about a close call
daily.description: Telling a friend about something that almost went wrong.
daily.example: I slipped on the stairs and almost fell down.

daily.description: A friend's reminder saved you.
daily.example: Good thing you told me. I almost forgot.

daily.title: Relief while shopping
daily.description: Said when you almost bought the wrong thing.
daily.example: If I hadn't checked the size, I would have bought the wrong one.

work.description: Explaining to your boss that you almost made an error but caught it in time.
work.example: When I checked, I realized I had almost sent the wrong documents.

work.title: Thanking a coworker
work.description: A coworker helped you meet a deadline.
work.example: Thanks to Tanaka-san, I was saved. I nearly missed the deadline.

etymology: It comes from 「〜ところだ」 (about to) plus the past 「だった」: “I was at the stage of about to ... (but it didn't happen)”. From this came the meaning “nearly ...”.

similar.title: 〜そうになる
similar.explanation: Both can be translated as "almost ...". 「〜そうになった」 focuses on the signs that appeared at the time, usually an involuntary reaction (「泣きそうになった」「転びそうになった」); 「〜ところだった」 stresses that it was "just one step from becoming reality", and often pairs with 「もう少しで」 or 「〜なかったら」.

similar.title: 〜かける・〜かけの
similar.explanation: 「死にかけた」 and 「溺れかけた」 also mean "almost ...", but 「〜かける」 focuses on the thing having already started and being halfway through; 「〜ところだった」 focuses on the thing not having happened at all, with a sense of relief: "that was close".

similar.title: 〜ところだ
similar.explanation: Same root. 「〜ところだ」 describes the stage an action is at (about to / in the middle of / just finished); "dictionary form + 「ところだった」" extends "was about to ..." into "almost ...".

formation: 「〜ところだった」 = 「〜ところだ」 (verb dictionary form + 「ところ」 = "at the point where ... is about to happen") + the past form 「だった」. Literally it's "I was at the point where ... was about to happen". Since it stops at the "about to" point, it implies that the event never actually happened. Add 「もう少しで」「危うく」 or 「〜なかったら」, and "one step away, but it didn't happen" comes to the fore, giving "almost ...". Without such words, and with no danger in the context, it's simply the past of 「〜ところだ」: "I was about to ...".

meaning: A situation keeps changing in one direction with no sign of stopping. Like “more and more ...” or “keeps ...ing”.
connection: Dictionary form of a verb of change + 一方だ

senses.label: More and more ...
senses.meaning: Things keep moving in only one direction. Often used for bad changes such as increasing, decreasing or getting worse. It follows verbs of change like 「増える」, 「減る」, 「なる」 or 「上がる」.
senses.connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) + 一方だ (common: 「増える一方だ」, 「悪くなる一方だ」, 「〜ていく一方だ」)
examples: Prices just keep going up.
Lately my work keeps increasing, so I don't even have time to rest.
This town's population keeps shrinking.

senses.label: Past and modifying forms
senses.meaning: It can also be used in the past, 「一方だった」, or before a noun as 「〜一方の」. The meaning stays the same: a steady one-way change.
senses.connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) + 一方だった / 一方である
examples: My father's condition kept getting worse.
Relations between the two countries are steadily deteriorating.

notes: It must follow a verb that expresses change (「増える」「減る」「悪くなる」「広がる」): ✕「勉強する一方だ」 ✕「忙しい一方だ」→ ○「忙しくなる一方だ」.
Add one 「で」 and the meaning changes completely: 「物価は上がる一方だ」 (prices keep rising); 「物価が上がる一方で、給料は上がらない」 (prices are rising, while wages aren't).

This expression often carries a helpless sense of "it can't be stopped, with no sign of improvement". Saying 「売上は減る一方です」 to a client or boss sounds pessimistic; in formal settings, people often say 「減少傾向にあります」 instead.

daily.title: Complaining about prices
daily.description: Chatting with family about living costs.
daily.example: Vegetable prices just keep going up, don't they?

daily.title: Talking about weight
daily.description: Telling a friend about your recent weight change.
daily.example: I don't exercise, so my weight just keeps going up.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: News often uses it for social problems that keep getting worse.
daily.example: The number of empty houses keeps rising across the country.

work.title: Sales report
work.description: Explaining in a meeting that sales keep falling.
work.example: For the past six months, sales have kept falling.

work.title: Explaining a staff shortage
work.description: Telling your boss about workload and staffing.
work.example: The workload keeps growing, but our staff numbers are going down.

etymology: 「一方」 originally means “one direction, one side”. 「〜一方だ」 is “(changing) in only one direction”, so it expresses change that keeps going one way.

similar.title: 〜ばかりだ (increasingly)
similar.explanation: Both express continuous change in one direction and are often interchangeable. 「〜ばかりだ」 is used almost only for bad changes and carries the speaker's dissatisfaction or worry; 「〜一方だ」 is relatively objective and also works for neutral changes (「人気は高まる一方だ」).

similar.title: 〜つつある
similar.explanation: Both describe change in progress. 「〜つつある」 only says "is gradually ...ing", with no sense of "it won't stop", and is written and neutral; 「〜一方だ」 stresses moving in only one direction with no sign of turning back.

similar.title: 〜一方（で）
similar.explanation: Same root (both use 「一方」). 「〜一方で」 is followed by another clause and means "on one hand ..., on the other ..."; 「〜一方だ」 ends the sentence with 「だ」 and means "more and more ...".

formation: 「一方」 = "one" + "direction", i.e. "a single direction". Put a change verb in the dictionary form before it and add the copula 「だ」, and it literally says "(this change) is in a single direction". "Only one direction" means no turning back and no stopping, so it expresses change that keeps going one way: "more and more ...", "keeps ...ing". And because it's about "direction", it must follow a change verb that has a direction built in; an action like 「勉強する」 doesn't involve change, so it has no direction and can't be used.

meaning: The same subject has two sides or does two things in parallel, or two different situations are contrasted. Like “on one hand ..., on the other hand ...” or “while ...”.
connection: Verb / adjective plain form (な-adjective + な / である; noun + である) + 一方(で); at the start of a sentence: 「一方」, 「その一方で」

senses.label: Doing two things
senses.meaning: The same person or thing does two things or has two sides at the same time. The two parts are simply listed, with no strong opposition. Like “while also ...” or “besides ...ing”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + 一方(で)
examples: He works at a company while also attending university at night.
My mother handles the housework and also volunteers in the community.

senses.label: Contrasting two sides
senses.meaning: Contrasts two opposite sides of the same thing, or two different situations. Like “on the other hand” or “whereas”. Often used for pros and cons.
senses.connection: Plain form (な-adjective + な / である; noun + である) + 一方(で)
examples: This job pays well, but on the other hand there are few days off.
The city is convenient, but the cost of living is high.
While exports are increasing, imports are decreasing.

senses.label: Sentence-initial: on the other hand
senses.meaning: At the start of a sentence as 「一方、」 or 「その一方で」, it follows on from the previous sentence and introduces a contrast. Mostly written language and news.
senses.connection: (Previous sentence.) + 一方、/ その一方で、+ next sentence
examples: The population is growing in urban areas. Meanwhile, rural areas are becoming depopulated.
Life has become more convenient. On the other hand, human connections are weakening.

notes: The most common mistakes are with nouns and na-adjectives: nouns take 「である一方」, and na-adjectives take 「な一方」 or 「である一方」. ✕「学生の一方で」→ ○「学生である一方で」; ✕「便利一方」→ ○「便利な一方」.
Drop 「で」 and end with 「だ」, and the meaning becomes "more and more ...": 「物価が上がる一方で、給料は横ばいだ」 (contrast) is completely different from 「物価は上がる一方だ」 (prices keep rising).
Don't mix it up with 「反面」: 「反面」 can only contrast the good and bad sides of the same thing; to contrast two different people or things, use 「一方で」. ✕「兄は背が高い反面、弟は低い」→ ○「兄は背が高い一方で、弟は低い」.

etymology: 「一方」 originally means “one direction, one side”. 「〜一方で」 is “on this side ... (on the other side ...)”, which led to the meanings of parallel actions and contrast.

similar.title: 〜反面
similar.explanation: Both can contrast two sides. 「〜反面」 is specifically for the positive and negative sides of the same thing (「便利な反面、危険もある」); 「〜一方で」 is more widely used and can also contrast two different things, or express doing two things at the same time.

similar.title: 〜に対して
similar.explanation: Both can contrast two situations. 「AはXのに対して、BはY」 stresses a sharp difference between A and B; 「〜一方で」 is milder and can either contrast or simply list side by side.

similar.title: 〜ながら
similar.explanation: Both can be translated as "while ...". 「〜ながら」 means doing two actions at the very same moment (「音楽を聞きながら勉強する」); 「〜一方で」 means doing two things in parallel over a period of time (「働く一方で、大学に通う」), not necessarily at the same moment.

similar.title: 〜一方だ
similar.explanation: Same root (both use 「一方」). 「〜一方だ」 ends the sentence with 「だ」 and means "more and more ..."; 「〜一方で」 must always be followed by another clause.

formation: 「一方」 = "one side, one aspect". Add 「で」, which marks a place or state, and you get "on this side ...". Once you've said "this side", the listener naturally expects "the other side", so another clause must follow, forming an "on one hand ..., on the other ..." structure. If both sides are two activities of the same subject, it becomes "while (also) ..."; if the two sides are opposite in nature, it becomes a contrast: "whereas ...". Put 「一方」 on its own at the start of a sentence (「一方、」「その一方で」), and you're treating the previous sentence as "this side" and turning to "the other side".

meaning: As the first thing changes, the second changes accordingly. It also means acting according to rules or instructions. Like “as ...” or “in accordance with ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + にしたがって (written: にしたがい)

senses.label: As ...
senses.meaning: As the first thing changes or develops, the second changes along with it. Both parts are changes.
senses.connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) / noun expressing change + にしたがって
examples: As you climb the mountain, the temperature drops.
As the times have changed, people's values have changed too.
As I've gotten older, my stamina has declined.

senses.label: According to ...
senses.meaning: Acting by following rules, instructions, orders or customs. Like “following ...” or “in accordance with ...”. It often follows nouns like 「指示」, 「規則」, 「矢印」 or 「案内」.
senses.connection: Noun (指示・規則・ルール・案内 etc.) + にしたがって + action
examples: Please evacuate following the staff's instructions.
Please follow the arrows.

notes: In the "as ..." sense, the second part can't be the speaker's intention or an order: ✕「年をとるにしたがって、運動しよう」→ ○「年をとるにしたがって、体力が落ちてきた」.
In the "as ..." sense, both parts must be gradual changes; a one-time event doesn't work: ✕「卒業するにしたがって、就職した」→ ○「卒業とともに就職した」.
「指示に従ってください」 is common in announcements and notices, but saying 「私に従ってください」 face to face to a customer sounds commanding and harsh. In service situations, say 「ご案内いたします」 or 「こちらへどうぞ」.

etymology: 「したがう」 is written 「従う」 and originally means “to follow, to obey”. 「〜にしたがって」 is “following along with ...”, which gave two meanings: “as (something changes)” and “according to (rules)”.

similar.title: 〜につれて
similar.explanation: In the "as ..." sense the two are basically interchangeable. 「〜につれて」 is more conversational and only expresses proportional change, with no "according to" meaning; 「〜にしたがって」 can also mean following rules or instructions (「規則に従って」).

similar.title: 〜に伴って
similar.explanation: Both can mean "as ...". 「〜に伴って」 is more formal and can also express a one-time accompanying event (「法改正に伴って手続きが変わる」); 「〜にしたがって」 leans toward gradual, proportional change.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: Both can be translated as "according to, based on". 「〜に基づいて」 means making a judgment or producing something based on data, facts or laws (「データに基づいて分析する」); 「〜に従って」 means acting in obedience to rules or instructions (「指示に従って避難する」).

similar.title: 〜とおりに
similar.explanation: Both can be translated as "according to". 「〜とおりに」 stresses doing it "exactly as, just like" (「説明書のとおりに組み立てる」); 「〜に従って」 stresses obeying and complying (「ルールに従って」).

formation: 「〜にしたがって」 = the case particle 「に」 (target) + the te-form of the verb 「従う」 (to follow, to obey). The original meaning of 「Aに従う」 is "to walk behind A, to do as A says". When A is a rule, an instruction or an arrow, it means "(acting) according to A"; when A is something that keeps changing, "following along with it" becomes "as A changes, B changes along with it". Because it's "following", A comes first and B comes after, with B's change depending on A. So it expresses synchronized, gradual, proportional change, and the second part can't be the speaker's own decision.

meaning: As the first thing changes, the second gradually changes along with it. Like “as ...”.
connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) / noun expressing change + につれて (written: につれ)

senses.label: As ...
senses.meaning: A change in the first part drives a change in the second, and both progress step by step in proportion. Both parts express change. Like “as ..., gradually ...”.
senses.connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) + につれて (common: 「時間が経つにつれて」, 「年をとるにつれて」)
examples: As time passed, the sadness faded too.
As my Japanese improved, life in Japan became more fun.
As I've gotten older, I've come to remember the past more often.

senses.label: With nouns of change
senses.meaning: It can follow nouns that already contain the idea of change, such as 「成長」, 「変化」, 「発展」 or 「進歩」.
senses.connection: Noun of change + につれて
examples: As the economy developed, people's lives became richer.
As the children grew, the house started to feel smaller.

notes: The second part must also be a gradual change, not a one-time action or the speaker's intention: ✕「暗くなるにつれて、家に帰ろう」→ ○「暗くなるにつれて、人通りが少なくなった」.
When it follows a noun, the noun itself must imply change: ✕「雨につれて」 ✕「年につれて」→ ○「年をとるにつれて」「時代の変化につれて」.
「につれて」 only means "as ...", never "according to": ✕「規則につれて行動する」→ ○「規則に従って行動する」.
The 「連れて」 in 「子どもを連れて行く」 means "taking someone along"; that's not this grammar point.

etymology: 「つれる」 is written 「連れる」 and originally means “to take along, accompany”. 「〜につれて」 is “being taken along by ...”, so one change drags another along with it. As a grammar pattern it is usually written in kana.

similar.title: 〜にしたがって
similar.explanation: Interchangeable in the "as ..." sense. 「〜にしたがって」 is slightly more formal and also means "according to rules or instructions"; 「〜につれて」 only expresses proportional change.

similar.title: 〜に伴って
similar.explanation: Both can mean "as ...". 「〜に伴って」 is more formal and can express a one-time accompanying event (「法律改正に伴って手続きが変わる」); 「〜につれて」 stresses gradual, continuous change.

similar.title: 〜とともに
similar.explanation: Both can mean "as ...". 「〜とともに」 is more formal and can also mean "together with" or "at the same time as"; 「〜につれて」 has only the "as ..." meaning and is more common in conversation.

similar.title: 〜ば〜ほど
similar.explanation: Both express two quantities changing together. 「〜ば〜ほど」 means "the more ..., the more ...", stressing a proportional relationship of degree, and the second part can be an evaluation (「考えれば考えるほど分からなくなる」); 「〜につれて」 focuses on the process of change as time passes.

formation: 「〜につれて」 = the case particle 「に」 + the te-form of the verb 「つれる」 (「連れる」: to take someone along). 「AにつれてB」 literally means "B is taken along by A": when A moves forward, B moves with it. So both parts must be things that are "moving, changing", and B's change is pulled along by A, in sync and gradually. A one-time action or the speaker's own decision isn't a change that is "taken along", so it can't be the second part. As a grammar point its meaning has become abstract, so it's usually written in kana: 「につれて」.

meaning: Means “together with ...”, and also “as ...” or “at the same time as ...”. More formal than 「と一緒に」.
connection: Noun + とともに; verb dictionary form, い-adjective, noun + である + とともに

senses.label: Together with ...
senses.meaning: Doing something together with someone or something. The formal version of 「〜と一緒に」, common in speeches, news and writing.
senses.connection: Noun (person, organization, etc.) + とともに
examples: I welcomed the new year with my family.
We will work on community development together with all of you in the area.

senses.label: As ...
senses.meaning: As the first thing changes, the second changes too. Both parts are changes. Close in meaning to 「〜につれて」, but more formal.
senses.connection: Verb of change (dictionary form) / noun of change + とともに
examples: As I've gotten older, my memory has weakened.
As the economy developed, environmental problems became serious.

senses.label: At the same time as ...
senses.meaning: Two things happen at the same time, or the same thing has two sides at once. Like “at the same time as ...” or “both ... and ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + とともに; noun / な-adjective + であるとともに
examples: I decided to go back to my hometown upon graduating.
When the exam ended I felt relieved, and at the same time a little lonely.
He is both a doctor and a writer.

notes: When a noun or na-adjective means "is both ... and ...", you must add 「である」, or the meaning changes completely: 「医者とともに」 means "together with a doctor"; to say "is both a doctor and a writer", say 「医者であるとともに、作家でもある」.
The "together with" meaning is very formal. Saying 「友達とともに昼ご飯を食べた」 to a friend in everyday life sounds like a speech script; in conversation use 「友達と一緒に」.

The three meanings are told apart by the word before it: a person or organization → "together with" (「家族とともに」); something that changes → "as ..." (「発展とともに」); a one-time event → "at the same time as" (「卒業とともに」).

etymology: 「とも」 is written 「共」 and means “together, jointly”. 「と＋共に」 is “together with ...”, and from “jointly” came the meanings “at the same time” and “as ...”.

similar.title: 〜と同時に
similar.explanation: Both can mean "at the same time". 「〜と同時に」 stresses that the moments are almost exactly the same; 「〜とともに」 also means "together" and "as ...", so it covers a wider range.

similar.title: 〜につれて
similar.explanation: Similar in the "as ..." sense. 「〜につれて」 stresses gradual, proportional change and is more conversational; 「〜とともに」 is more formal and also works for one-time simultaneous events (「卒業とともに帰国した」).

similar.title: 〜に伴って
similar.explanation: Both can mean "as, along with". 「〜に伴って」 can only be used with events, not to mean "together with someone"; 「〜とともに」 can (「仲間とともに戦う」).

formation: 「〜とともに」 = the case particle 「と」 (companion) + 「共（とも）」 (jointly, together) + 「に」 (making it adverbial). The basic meaning of 「Aとともに」 is "jointly, together with A". When A is a person, it means "doing something together with A"; when A is an event, "(happening) together with that event" becomes "at the same time as ..."; when A is an ongoing change, "changing together with that change" becomes "as ...". All three meanings come from the core idea of "together, being in the same place"; only the kind of A differs, so to tell the meaning, look at what A is first.

meaning: Two things happen at almost the same moment, or the same thing has two qualities at once. Like “at the same time as ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / noun + と同時に; noun / な-adjective + であると同時に

senses.label: At the same moment
senses.meaning: As soon as the first thing happens, the second happens too, with almost no gap in time. Like “the moment ...” or “as soon as ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + と同時に; noun + と同時に (「発売と同時に」, 「到着と同時に」)
examples: The moment the bell rang, the students rushed out of the classroom.
The new game sold out as soon as it was released.
It started to rain just as I got home.

senses.label: Both at once
senses.meaning: The same thing has two qualities or roles at once, or two feelings arise together. Like “both ... and ...” or “while also ...”.
senses.connection: Noun / な-adjective + であると同時に; verb / adjective plain form + と同時に
examples: He is a teacher and, at the same time, the father of two children.
I'm happy I passed, but at the same time I'm a little anxious.

notes: When a noun or na-adjective means "is both ... and ...", you must add 「である」: 「教師と同時に」 would be understood as "at the same time as the teacher"; to say "is both a teacher and a father", say 「教師であると同時に、父親でもある」.
It's most easily confused with 「たとたん」: the second part of 「たとたん」 can't be an intention or an order, but the second part of 「と同時に」 can. ✕「チャイムが鳴ったとたん、書き始めてください」→ ○「チャイムが鳴ると同時に、書き始めてください」.
The standalone adverb 「同時に」 (「二つのことを同時にする」) is not this grammar point.

etymology: 「同時」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “the same time”. 「〜と同時に」 is “at the same moment as ...”, and from timing it extended to “having two sides at once”.

similar.title: 〜とともに
similar.explanation: Both can mean "at the same time". 「〜とともに」 can also mean "together" and "as ...", so its range is wider; 「〜と同時に」 only means "at the same time", with a stronger sense of timing being identical.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: Both mean "as soon as ...". With 「〜たとたん」, the second part is something unexpected that happens, not the speaker's intentional action; 「〜と同時に」 has no sense of surprise, and the second part can be a deliberate action or an instruction.

similar.title: 〜次第 (as soon as)
similar.explanation: Both can mean "as soon as ...". 「〜次第」 means "once the first part is done, the second will be done right away"; the second part is the speaker's intentional action, often in business (「届き次第ご連絡します」). 「〜と同時に」 only says that two things happen at the same time.

similar.title: 〜一方（で）
similar.explanation: Similar when meaning "having two aspects at once". 「〜一方で」 focuses on contrasting the two sides; 「〜と同時に」 focuses on the two sides coexisting (「うれしいと同時に、不安もある」).

formation: 「〜と同時に」 = the case particle 「と」 (the thing compared, the thing that is the same) + the Sino-Japanese word 「同時」 (the same moment) + 「に」 (making it adverbial). 「Aと同時に」 literally means "at the same moment as A". When A is an event, it means two things happen with almost no time gap; when A is an identity or quality, as in "being ..." (「〜であると同時に」), "holding true at the same moment" becomes "having two identities or two feelings at once". Because it only says "the timing is the same" and contains no sense of surprise, the second part can be a deliberate action or an instruction.

meaning: A situation continues or is spread over a rough range between two points in time or two places. Like “from ... through ...” or “in the area from ... to ...”.
connection: Noun (time / place) + から + noun (time / place) + にかけて

senses.label: Range of time
senses.meaning: Shows a rough period of time. Unlike 「〜から〜まで」, the start and end are not exact; it stresses “during this stretch”. Common in weather forecasts, seasons and how long events last.
senses.connection: Time noun + から + time noun + にかけて (「今夜から明日にかけて」, 「3月から5月にかけて」)
examples: Heavy rain is expected from tonight through tomorrow morning.
Cherry blossoms bloom from the end of March to early April.
The shop is closed over the New Year holidays.

senses.label: Range of places
senses.meaning: Shows a rough geographical area, the stretch from one place to another. Common when describing weather, disasters or distribution.
senses.connection: Place noun + から + place noun + にかけて (「関東から東北にかけて」)
examples: Heavy rain fell over a wide area from Kyushu to Kanto.
I have pain from my shoulders down my back.

senses.label: Without the start point
senses.meaning: Sometimes 「から」 is left out and only 「〜にかけて」 is used, meaning “(continuing) toward ...”. Common in weather forecasts.
senses.connection: Time noun + にかけて (「夕方にかけて」, 「週末にかけて」)
examples: The rain is expected to get heavier toward the evening.
Temperatures will likely drop toward the weekend.

notes: It can't be used for concrete schedules with clear start and end points: ✕「9時から10時にかけて会議をする」→ ○「9時から10時まで会議をする」.
If you use 「〜から〜にかけて」 when sending a notice to a client or boss, or when setting a time, they won't know the exact time. For formal notices, use 「〜から〜まで」 to state the start and end clearly.
「〜にかけては」 (「料理にかけては誰にも負けない」) means "when it comes to ...", which is completely different from this grammar point.

etymology: 「かける」 is written 「掛ける」 and has the sense of “to span, to stretch across”. 「〜から〜にかけて」 originally meant “stretching from ... to ...”, that is, “spanning this range”, so it shows a rough interval.

similar.title: 〜から〜まで
similar.explanation: Both mean "from ... to ...". 「〜から〜まで」 has a clear start and end point and works for concrete actions (「9時から5時まで働く」); 「〜から〜にかけて」 has a vague range and mostly describes continuing or spread-out states (rain, flowers, pain).

similar.title: 〜にわたって
similar.explanation: Both express a span of time or space. 「〜にわたって」 stresses that the whole range is covered and that the scale is large (「3日間にわたって会議が続いた」); 「〜にかけて」 only gives a rough range.

similar.title: 〜にかけては
similar.explanation: Same root (both come from 「掛ける」), but the meanings differ: 「〜にかけては」 means "when it comes to ... (being best at it)"; this grammar point expresses a range.

formation: 「〜から〜にかけて」 = 「から」 (starting point) + 「〜に」 (endpoint) + the te-form of 「かける」 (「掛ける」: to span, to lay across). 「AからBにかけて」 literally means "laid across from A to B". Like a bridge spanning A and B, the focus is on the stretch in between, not on the two ends. So neither the start nor the end is exact, and it means "roughly in the area / period from A to B". Because it describes a whole stretch, the second part is usually a state that continues or is spread across that range (rain, blooming flowers, pain), not a one-time concrete action.

meaning: Something is done or happens with a person, place or thing as its center or main focus. Like “centered on ...” or “mainly ...”.
connection: Noun + を中心に(して) / を中心として / を中心とした + noun

senses.label: Centered on ...
senses.meaning: A place or person is the center in space or in an organization, and things revolve around it.
senses.connection: Noun + を中心に(して) / を中心として
examples: The earth revolves around the sun.
This team is united around Tanaka-san.
Shopping streets spread out around the station.

senses.label: Mainly ...
senses.meaning: A certain range or content is the main focus, but not the only thing. Often used for where something is popular, what an activity covers, or which areas were hit by a disaster.
senses.connection: Noun + を中心に + verb; noun + を中心とした + noun
examples: This anime is popular mainly among young people.
This exam will focus mainly on grammar.
Heavy snow fell in areas centered on the Kanto region.

notes: To modify a noun, use 「を中心とした／を中心とする」: ✕「関東を中心に地域で大雪が降った」→ ○「関東を中心とした地域で大雪が降った」.
「を中心に」 means "mainly ..., but also including other things", not "only": 「文法を中心に出題する」 implies other things will be tested too. To say only grammar will be tested, say 「文法だけ出題する」.
The 「の中心に」 in 「公園の中心に噴水がある」 means "in the very center of ..."; that's not this grammar point.

etymology: 「中心」 is a Sino-Japanese word meaning “center, core”. 「〜を中心に（する）」 is “making ... the center”, which extended from a spatial center to the main focus of content or scope.

similar.title: 〜をはじめ
similar.explanation: These two are often compared. 「〜をはじめ」 first names the most representative item, and the point is that "there are many more of the same kind" (「社長をはじめ、全員が出席した」); 「〜を中心に」 stresses where the core or focus is, with everything else revolving around it.

similar.title: 〜をめぐって
similar.explanation: Both can be translated as "around ...". 「〜をめぐって」 is followed by disputes, conflict or discussion (「遺産をめぐって争う」); 「〜を中心に」 is followed by activity, distribution or popularity centered on something, with no sense of dispute.

formation: 「〜を中心に」 = the object particle 「を」 + the noun 「中心」 (center) + 「に（する）」. 「AをBにする」 is the pattern "treat A as B", so 「Aを中心にする」 means "treat A as the center". A "center" is a point with things around it, so this grammar point can express revolving around something in space (「太陽を中心に回る」) as well as "mainly A, with other things alongside" in content. Because it comes from 「〜にする」, you can also say 「を中心にして」 or 「を中心として」, and to modify a noun you use 「を中心とした／を中心とする」.

meaning: Names the most representative example and shows there are others of the same kind. Like “starting with ...” or “..., as well as ...”.
connection: Noun + をはじめ(として) / をはじめとする + noun

senses.label: Starting with ...
senses.meaning: First names the main or most typical item, then mentions others of the same kind. The second part often has words of scope like 「など」, 「多くの」, 「さまざまな」 or 「皆」.
senses.connection: Noun + をはじめ(として)、…など / 皆
examples: Starting with the president, all the employees attended the meeting.
Kyoto has many famous temples, starting with Kinkaku-ji.
I'm studying Japanese, as well as Korean and Chinese.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜をはじめとする＋noun」 or 「〜をはじめとした＋noun」 modifies the following noun: “... such as, led by ...”. Mostly written language.
senses.connection: Noun + をはじめとする / をはじめとした + noun
examples: In big cities such as Tokyo, rent is expensive.
Japanese food, with sushi as a prime example, is popular overseas too.

notes: The second part must be a group of the same kind that includes A; you can't just mention A alone: ✕「社長をはじめ、会議に出席した」→ ○「社長をはじめ、役員全員が会議に出席した」.

What comes before 「をはじめ」 should be the highest-ranking, most representative member of the group. In a speech, 「社長をはじめ、社員の皆様」 is appropriate; putting someone of lower rank first (✕「新入社員をはじめ、社長も」) would be seen as rude in Japan.
「仕事を始める」 (start work) is a verb, not this grammar point. This grammar point is followed by 「、」 or 「として／とする」 and then lists more of the same kind.

etymology: 「はじめ」 is written 「始め」, a noun formed from the stem of the verb 「始める」, meaning “the beginning, the first one”. 「〜をはじめ」 is “taking ... as the first (in a list)”, hence “starting with ...”.

similar.title: 〜を中心に
similar.explanation: These two are often compared. 「〜を中心に」 stresses the core or focus, with everything else on the periphery; 「〜をはじめ」 simply puts the most representative item first, and the point is that many more of the same kind follow.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: Both are used for listing. 「〜や〜など」 lists examples side by side, all with equal status, and is common in conversation too; 「〜をはじめ」 highlights the first item as the most important and representative, and sounds more formal.

similar.title: 〜はもとより・〜はもちろん
similar.explanation: Both can mean "not only A, but also B ...". 「Aはもとより B も」 stresses "A goes without saying, and even B ...", with the focus on extending the range to B; 「Aをはじめ」 makes A the representative of a group, with the focus on "many, including A".

similar.title: 〜始める
similar.explanation: Same root (both come from the verb 「始める」). 「〜始める」 attaches to a verb and means "start ...ing" (「雨が降り始めた」); 「〜をはじめ」 has become an abstract listing pattern and no longer means "start".

formation: 「〜をはじめ」 = the object particle 「を」 + 「はじめ」 (「始め」, the noun made from the stem of the verb 「始める」, meaning "the beginning, the first one"). 「Aをはじめ」 can be understood as "with A as the first (and counting on from there)". If there's a "first", there must be a second and a third, so the second part must be a group of the same kind that includes A; and what gets placed "first" is usually the most important, most representative one. Add 「として」 or 「とする」 (treat as) and it becomes "... with A as the first"; to modify a noun, use 「をはじめとする」.

meaning: Putting a feeling, wish or intention into an action or thing. Like “with (love, gratitude) ...” or “full of ...”.
connection: Noun (心・愛・感謝・願い・思い etc.) + を込めて / を込めた + noun

senses.label: Doing with feeling
senses.meaning: Doing something with a certain feeling or intention. It usually follows nouns of feeling like 「心」, 「愛」, 「感謝」, 「願い」, 「思い」 or 「祈り」.
senses.connection: Noun of feeling + を込めて + verb (「心を込めて作る」, 「感謝を込めて贈る」)
examples: I put my heart into making a cake for my mother.
I wrote the letter with feelings of gratitude.
We rang the bell with a wish for peace.

senses.label: Filled with ...
senses.meaning: 「〜を込めた＋noun」 means “(something) filled with ...”. The passive 「〜が込められている」 shows that a work contains a certain feeling.
senses.connection: Noun of feeling + を込めた + noun; noun + が込められている
examples: This is a sweater my grandmother knitted by hand with love.
I threw the ball with all my strength.

notes: It follows feelings, intentions or 「力」. To put a physical object into something, use 「入れる」: ✕「砂糖を込めてケーキを作った」→ ○「砂糖を入れて」; ○「心を込めてケーキを作った」.
Attitudes like 「自信」「勇気」「誇り」 take 「を持って」, not 「を込めて」: ✕「自信を込めて話す」→ ○「自信を持って話す」.
To say "(a work) contains ..." in the passive, use 「が込められている」: ✕「この名前には親の願いを込められている」→ ○「この名前には親の願いが込められている」.

etymology: 「こめる」 is written 「込める」 (older 「籠める」) and originally means “to load, to pack in”, as in 「弾を込める」 (load a bullet). From “putting something in” it came to mean “putting feelings into” something.

similar.title: 〜つもりで
similar.explanation: Both mean doing something with a certain mindset. 「〜つもりで」 means "with the intention or attitude of ..." (「死ぬつもりで頑張る」), focusing on resolve and intention; 「〜を込めて」 means pouring feelings or care into an action or a work, focusing on the emotion invested.

similar.title: 〜込む
similar.explanation: Same root (「込める」 is the transitive counterpart of 「込む」). 「〜込む」 attaches to a verb and means "go into, put into, go deep" (「飛び込む」「考え込む」); 「〜を込めて」 swaps what's put in for feelings, meaning "pouring one's heart into".

formation: 「〜を込めて」 = the object particle 「を」 + the te-form of the verb 「込める」 (to load, to pack in). 「込める」 originally means putting something into a container, as in 「弾を込める」 (load a bullet). Swap what's put in for 「心」「愛」「感謝」「願い」, and it becomes "putting feelings into (an action or work)", i.e. "full of ..., with all one's ...". Since "putting in" needs a container, there is always an action or work that carries the feeling (「作る」「書く」「贈る」「歌う」); the passive 「〜が込められている」 means that a certain feeling is "packed inside" the work.

meaning: Expresses that something is done by using a person or thing as a medium or means (“through…”, “via…”), and also that something holds throughout a whole period or range (“all through…”). 「を通して」 is more common in speech, 「を通じて」 in writing, and 「を通じた」 modifies a noun.
connection: Noun (person / medium / activity) + を通して／を通じて (modifying a noun: を通じた); noun of time or range (一年・生涯・全国) + を通して／を通じて
etymology: 「通す」 means “to pass something through” and 「通じる」 (old 「通ず」) means “to lead to, to connect”; both carry the sense of “going from one end to the other, running through”. From “passing through something to the other side” it extended to “via some medium”, and from “running through from start to finish” to “throughout a period”.
formation: 「〜を通して／〜を通じて」 is the object marker 「を」 plus the て-form of the verb 「通す」 (to pass through) or 「通じる」 (to connect, lead to). Literally 「Aを通して」 is “passing (the matter) through A”: A is like a pipe or a bridge through which information, experience or contact reaches the other end, so with people, media or activities it means “through… (means, medium, intermediary)”. If A is a period or range, “passing through from start to end” becomes “throughout that period or range”, which is why the same form also expresses a whole duration. 「通じる」 is intransitive (naturally running through) while 「通す」 is transitive (making it run through), so 「を通して」 carries a slightly more deliberate “making use of” nuance and 「を通じて」 is more neutral and written. The 「を」 marks the thing passed through, the same use as in 「公園を通る」.

senses.label: Through (a means)
senses.meaning: Getting a result by means of an experience, activity or medium. Like “through ...”.
senses.connection: Noun (経験・活動・テレビ・インターネット etc.) + を通して / を通じて
examples: I learned many things through studying abroad.
Through the internet, you can interact with people all over the world.
Interaction through social media is spreading.

senses.label: Through a person
senses.meaning: Communicating or making contact through an intermediary. Like “via ...”. More indirect and formal than contacting someone directly.
senses.connection: Person / organization noun + を通して / を通じて + 伝える / 申し込む etc.
examples: Through a senior colleague, I was able to meet the president.
We will contact you with the details through my secretary.

senses.label: Throughout
senses.meaning: After a noun of time or range, it means “all through the whole ...”. Like “all year round” or “throughout ...”.
senses.connection: Time / range noun (一年・年間・生涯・全国 etc.) + を通して / を通じて
examples: This region is warm all year round.
Tourists visit this island throughout the year.
He called for peace throughout his life.

notes: To physically pass through a place, use 「を通って」, not 「を通して」: ✕「公園を通して駅へ行く」→ ○「公園を通って駅へ行く」.

When contacting someone through another person, 「〜を通して」 sounds formal and proper. In Japanese companies, going over your contact person or direct boss to reach someone higher up is considered rude, so formal requests often say 「〇〇さんを通してお願いする」.
In the passive, the agent takes 「によって」; with 「を通じて」 the meaning becomes “conveyed through someone”: ✕「この小説は村上春樹を通じて書かれた」 → ○「村上春樹によって書かれた」.
The 「通す」 in 「目を通す」 (look over), 「火を通す」 (cook through) and 「話を通す」 (put in a word beforehand) is a full verb, not this grammar point.
In the "throughout the whole period" sense, it must follow a period of time or a range (「一年」「年間」「生涯」): ✕「3時を通して」.

similar.title: 〜によって
similar.explanation: Both can express means or method. 「〜によって」 is more objective, pointing to the means or cause directly used (「機械によって作る」); 「〜を通して」 stresses going through an experience, a medium or an intermediary, with a sense of "passing through a process".

similar.title: 〜にわたって
similar.explanation: Both can express a time range. 「〜にわたって」 stresses the breadth of the range or length of time (「十年にわたって調査する」); 「〜を通じて」 stresses that a state continues “all the way through” (「一年を通じて温暖だ」).

similar.title: 〜を経て
similar.explanation: Both can be translated as "through, via". 「〜を経て」 means reaching the next step after passing through a place, stage or procedure (「審査を経て決定する」), focusing on the order of steps; 「〜を通して」 means using A as a channel or medium to achieve something.

similar.title: 〜通す
similar.explanation: Same root (both come from 「通す」). 「〜通す」 attaches to a verb and means carrying an action through to the end (「最後まで走り通す」); 「〜を通して」 follows a noun and expresses a means, a medium, or a whole period.
